When you create a generic class, the type arguments can go on the variable (`const users: Map<string, User> = new Map()`) or on the call (`const users = new Map<string, User>()`). Both give the same type. This rule picks one place. By default it is the call, which names the class once instead of twice.

Variables, class fields, and parameters with a default value are checked, except the parameters of arrow functions. Code that has type arguments on both sides, or on neither, is left alone.

`--fix` moves the type arguments to the other side.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 3} */}
```ts
const scores: Map<string, number> = new Map();

class Game {
  players: Set<string> = new Set();
}

function start(seen: Set<string> = new Set()) {}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```ts
const scores = new Map<string, number>();

class Game {
  players = new Set<string>();
}

function start(seen = new Set<string>()) {}
```

The annotation has to name the same class as the call. Here it does not, so moving the type arguments would change the type of the variable:

{/* good */}
```ts
const scores: ReadonlyMap<string, number> = new Map();
```

## Options

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `"constructor"` (default) | Type arguments go on the call: `new Map<string, number>()`. |
| `"type-annotation"` | Type arguments go on the annotation: `const scores: Map<string, number>`. |

{/* bad {"options": ["type-annotation"]} */}
```ts
const scores = new Map<string, number>();
```

{/* good {"options": ["type-annotation"]} */}
```ts
const scores: Map<string, number> = new Map();
```
